CAN.story:
In December 1975, in St John's, Newfoundland, Detective Robert Hillier was investigating Mount Cashel Orphanage, run by the Irish Christian Brothers. Two Brothers admitted molesting boys. The police chief and assistant chief ordered Hillier to stop. References to sexual assault were taken out of his report, the first version was destroyed, and the Justice Department laid no charges. Four Brothers were moved out of the province instead. In 1977 the Deputy Minister of Justice said further action was unwarranted. Police reopened the case only in February 1989, 14 years after the first report, and nine Brothers were convicted. The Hughes Royal Commission, one of the first official inquiries of its kind anywhere, found in 1991 that police and the Justice Department had not handled the files normally and that the child welfare director had insisted on special treatment for the Brothers. The province paid $11 million to more than 40 victims in 1997.

The same move-them-away habit shows up across the country. Fr Eric Dejaeger, an Oblate priest about to be charged in Igloolik, Nunavut, in 1995, fled to Belgium; Oblate officials said they knew he was leaving, and he lived 16 years in Oblate houses despite an international warrant. Returned in 2011, he was sentenced in 2015 to 19 years for 32 offences against Inuit children. Fr Johannes Rivoire left the Arctic for France in 1993. Canada issued warrants in 1998 and 2022, France refused extradition, and a 2024 review commissioned by the Oblates concluded he had assaulted six children. He died in France in 2024 without a trial. In 1994 Anglican priest Gordon Nakayama confessed to abusing minors; the church let him resign and did not tell police.

The state itself took children. In the Sixties Scoop, child welfare authorities removed thousands of Indigenous children and placed them with non-Indigenous families; an Ontario court ruled in 2017 that Ottawa had failed in its duty of care, and the government announced an agreement in principle worth about C$800 million. About 150,000 First Nations, Métis and Inuit children went through church-run residential schools; by the end of 2014, 37,951 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse. Under the settlement, claimants' records are to be destroyed after 19 September 2027 unless they ask to keep them. Canada also received children: 2,181 from South Korea between 1967 and 2008, and British "Home Children" sent under migration schemes that a UK inquiry later found exposed them to abuse.

Canada has also been a base for the trade. Azov Films in Toronto sold films of child exploitation to customers in over 50 countries; in 2013 police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued. Ontario removed the legal deadline (statute of limitations) for civil abuse claims in 2016.

When an abuser is moved, retired or allowed to resign quietly, the record often disappears with them. Ask who knew, whether police were told, and whether the files will still exist when survivors are ready to speak.

KOR.story:
In Busan, between 1975 and 1988, a state-backed facility called Brothers Home confined people labelled vagrants and forced them to work. Of 3,975 inmates in 1986, 3,117 had been brought in by police. The country's Truth and Reconciliation Commission counted 657 deaths there. An AP investigation in 2019 found the facility had also organised the adoption of 19 children abroad, and in 2025 the commission confirmed at least 31 children had been improperly sent overseas through it.

Brothers Home was one feeder into a much larger stream. About 163,898 South Korean children were sent abroad for adoption from 1953 to 2008: 109,242 to the United States, 11,165 to France, 9,297 to Denmark, 9,051 to Sweden, 6,295 to Norway, and thousands more to the Netherlands, Belgium, Australia and Canada. In 1974 South Korea tried to stop adoptions to Scandinavia; Swedish, Danish and Norwegian diplomats sent nine pleas, and it resumed. Adoptions peaked at 8,837 in 1985. In March 2025 the commission, reviewing petitions from 367 adoptees, found that agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign demand, registered children with known parents as orphans, and swapped identities when a child died before departure. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to welfare. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.

At the Gwangju Inhwa School for deaf students, a 2005 investigation found six staff, including the headmaster, had abused at least nine students. The teacher who alerted rights groups was fired, two abusers escaped because the statute of limitations (the legal deadline to prosecute) had run out, and appeal courts cut sentences to probation. Only after the 2011 film Silenced did the National Assembly remove that deadline for sex crimes against children under 13 and disabled people.

Online, Son Jong-woo ran Welcome to Video, a darknet site selling over 250,000 abuse videos for Bitcoin. US investigators traced payments to his server; 337 users were charged worldwide. He served 18 months in South Korea, and in 2020 the Seoul High Court refused to extradite him to the US. In the Telegram "Nth Room" and "Doctor's Room" chats, operators blackmailed at least 74 victims, 16 of them minors, into producing sexual images; Cho Ju-bin was sentenced to 40 years and Moon Hyung-wook to 34. By September 2024 police had handled more than 800 deepfake sex crime cases that year, most involving teenagers. The Korean Institute of Criminology said in 2013 that South Korean men are the main market for child sex tourism in Southeast Asia.

Each step here, from police roundups to adoption quotas to light sentences, was an official decision someone signed. When a country exports children or refuses to extradite an offender, ask who benefited and who checked the paperwork.

SWE.story:
In January 1975 South Korea tried to stop sending children to Scandinavia for adoption. The Swedish ambassador urged it to keep sending them, and it did. Between 1957 and 2005 Sweden received 9,051 Korean children. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found that Korean agencies had sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign demand and registered children with living parents as orphans.

Korea was not the only source. In Chile, children were taken from mainly poor mothers, some of whom were told their babies had died, and sent to families in the United States and Europe, including Sweden; the practice peaked under the Pinochet dictatorship. In Sri Lanka in the 1980s, babies were bought or taken from hospitals and handed to paid "acting mothers" who posed as birth mothers in court; some went to Sweden. Greek-born children, many labelled orphans after the civil war, were adopted into Sweden between 1950 and 1975.

Activism by Chilean adoptees pushed Sweden to open its own inquiry. Its report, issued on 2 June 2025 and nearly 1,600 pages long, reviewed 65 years of adoption and documented numerous irregularities and illegalities that state authorities had some knowledge of. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea in 2024.

Sweden also turns up in the online side of these cases. The Internet Watch Foundation actioned 6,820 web addresses hosted in Sweden in 2025, 2% of its total. Swedish police joined the international takedown of the Boystown platform in 2021 and a 2026 operation that arrested 28 men paying cryptocurrency for access to abuse forums.

A receiving country can look like the safe end of an adoption. The questions are what its officials were told about where the children came from, when they were told, and what they did with that knowledge.

MEX.story:
In 1976 a former seminarian named Juan Vaca wrote to the Vatican about Marcial Maciel, the Mexican priest who founded the Legion of Christ. More letters followed in 1978 and 1989, and formal charges were filed in 1998. None produced action. Only in 2006, 30 years after that first letter, did the Vatican order Maciel to retire to "prayer and penitence". He was never tried or removed from the priesthood. In 2019 the Legion's own report found 175 minors had been abused by 33 of its priests since 1941, at least 60 of them by Maciel, and that 14 of the abusive priests had themselves been abused inside the order.

Priests also moved across borders. In 1987 Fr Nicolás Aguilar Rivera was sent from Tehuacán to Los Angeles by his bishop; within a year 26 children were reported abused, and he fled back to Mexico before he could be arrested. In 2018 Costa Rican priest Mauricio Víquez fled accusations through Panama to Mexico, where he was caught and extradited in 2021; he was sentenced to 20 years.

In Cancún, hotelier Jean Succar Kuri was detained in the US in 2004 after complaints by several girls, and convicted in Mexico in 2011. Journalist Lydia Cacho's 2005 book linked his network to Puebla businessman Kamel Nacif and Governor Mario Marín. Puebla police then arrested Cacho and drove her about 900 miles to Puebla; leaked calls recorded Nacif and Marín discussing jailing her. In 2007 the Supreme Court ruled 6–4 that Marín had no case to answer. He was arrested in 2021 and is on trial for allegedly torturing Cacho; neither man has been convicted, and both are accused of torture, not of the abuse.

Children placed in shelters by the state were not safe either. In 2009, 14 children went missing from the church-run Casitas del Sur shelter, where Mexico City prosecutors had placed them, and a legislator accused officials of warning the shelter about searches. At La Gran Familia in Zamora, more than 40 parents' complaints had been filed before a 2014 raid freed 432 children. In 2020 the bishops' conference said 426 priests had been investigated over ten years; El Universal found only six sentences from 156 prosecutors' investigations between 2009 and 2019.

Here the people who raised the alarm, from seminarians to a journalist, faced more consequences than the accused. Notice how many complaints existed before anything was done, and ask who received them.

BEL.story:
In 1992 Belgium released Marc Dutroux early from a 13.5-year sentence for rape, over the objections of a prosecutor and a psychiatrist. In 1995 and 1996 he kidnapped six girls aged 8 to 19. His own mother wrote to authorities in 1995 that he was holding two girls. Police treated him as a prime suspect from June 1995 but took 14 months to arrest him. In the meantime they missed voices heard in his cellar and left videotapes unreviewed, while two police forces, the Gendarmerie and the judicial police, competed rather than cooperated. When the investigating judge was removed in October 1996 for attending a fundraising dinner for victims, hundreds of thousands of people joined the White March in Brussels. A parliamentary inquiry sharply criticised the police, and Belgium reorganised its police forces. In 2004 Dutroux was sentenced to life.

Witnesses later told investigators of abuse parties involving Dutroux and prominent people. These are the "X-dossiers". Prosecutors dismissed the statements, investigators were criticised for leading a key witness, and the claims of an elite network remain unproven. Unlike the police failures, they were never established.

The Catholic Church in Belgium faced its own count. A church commission set up in 2000 received 33 formal complaints, upheld 32, and found most were past the legal deadline to prosecute. A second commission in 2010 received 475 complaints in six months and linked 13 suicides to clerical abuse. Belgium also took in an abuser from abroad: Fr Eric Dejaeger fled Canada for Belgium in 1995 and lived 16 years in Oblate houses despite an international warrant. In 2014 the Flemish Parliament apologised for abuse in boarding schools and youth centres between 1930 and 1990. Belgium also received 3,697 children from South Korea, whose adoption system a 2025 Korean commission found riddled with false orphan papers.

The documented failures in the Dutroux case were ordinary ones: an early release, a mother's letter, unreviewed tapes, two rival police forces. When asking why abuse was not stopped, start with what was already on file.

COL.story:
In 1981 Colombian authorities uncovered a ring that had taken or bought hundreds of poor Andean children from their mothers and sold them abroad with forged papers, according to the New York Times. Adoptions abroad did not stop. The US issued 5,519 immigrant visas to children adopted from Bogotá between 1994 and 2014, and Colombia sent 20,864 children abroad from 2003 to 2022, one of the countries still open to intercountry adoption. In 2021 a Dutch government inquiry found "serious violations" in adoptions from countries including Colombia between 1967 and 1998, and that Dutch officials had known of wrongdoing for years without acting.

War has been another way children were taken. Colombia's Special Jurisdiction for Peace, a court set up under the peace deal, has identified a provisional count of 18,677 children recruited and used by the former FARC-EP guerrillas, and has indicted former commanders for war crimes including sexual violence against children. Former secretariat members have publicly acknowledged responsibility. The fighting has not ended for girls: the UN verified sexual violence against 33 girls in 2024, by the ELN, FARC dissident groups and the Clan del Golfo, and 26 cases in 2023, two of them by the Colombian armed forces.

Trafficking runs through tourist cities and border towns. In Cartagena, Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello, known as "La Madame", supplied young women and minors to parties on yachts and in hotels; prosecutors seized 15 ledgers of clients. She took a plea deal in 2018 for eight years and one month and was paroled in 2023. She said politicians were among her clients, a claim never verified. US men travelled repeatedly to Medellín to exploit girls, one of them 48 times in two years, and were prosecuted in Miami. The US 2025 trafficking report says Tren de Aragua moves displaced Venezuelan girls and women through Cúcuta, and that two complicit officials received plea sentences below the legal minimum.

The Catholic Church has never faced a national inquiry. In August 2020 the Constitutional Court ordered the Archdiocese of Medellín to disclose files on 915 accused clergy cases to a journalist within 48 hours; full compliance was not achieved.

Where no national inquiry exists, the only counts come from courts, the UN and reporters forcing files open. Ask who holds the records and why a court order was needed to see them.

VNM.story:
In April 1975, as South Vietnam was falling, President Ford directed $2 million in US aid to fly South Vietnamese orphans to the United States. Over 3,300 children were airlifted in Operation Babylift, and about 250 went to Australia. The first flight crash-landed shortly after take-off on 4 April, killing many children on board. A lawsuit later argued that many of the children were not orphans: poor families had sometimes placed children in orphanages without meaning to give them up, and many records lacked parental consent.

The adoption trade continued in peacetime. The US issued 7,498 visas to children adopted from Hanoi between 1994 and 2014, peaking at 828 in 2007. In April 2008 the US embassy reported that the number of babies said to be abandoned had risen 17-fold or more at orphanages in seven provinces. Vietnam let its US adoption agreement lapse that September. In 2009 a court in Nam Dinh tried 16 people, including the head of two social welfare centres and village clinic doctors and nurses, accused of soliciting infants from poor families and falsifying papers to say they were abandoned; 266 babies had been sent abroad from 2005 to 2008.

Vietnamese children are also moved out for other purposes. Ethnic Vietnamese girls, many sold by destitute families, filled brothels in Svay Pak, Cambodia. Hmong and other minority girls are lured or abducted to China for forced marriage. In the UK, Vietnamese children are exploited on cannabis farms and in nail bars, and many have gone missing from local-authority care. In 2011 Thai police freed 14 Vietnamese women, half of them pregnant, held by a company called Baby 101 that took orders for newborns.

Foreign offenders came in. After his 1999 UK conviction, singer Paul Gadd (Gary Glitter) was expelled from Cambodia and moved to Vietnam, where he was convicted in 2006 of obscene acts with girls aged 10 and 11. In 2007 an Australian group found 80 commercial cases of child exploitation by foreigners in Sa Pa, and Vietnam set up a child sex tourism unit that year.

A sudden rise in "abandoned" babies is a number someone should have questioned. When children leave a country in large numbers, ask who signed the papers that made them available.

ZWE.story:
In 1982 an internal report for the Iwerne Trust, which ran evangelical camps for boys in England, described how its former chair, the barrister John Smyth, had beaten boys and young men. The report's recipients did not go to the police. In 1984 Smyth moved to Zimbabwe, and in 1986 he founded Zambesi Ministries, which ran camps for boys. A 16-year-old died at one of those camps in December 1992. Smyth was arrested in 1997 but never charged in any country. Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, he moved to South Africa in 2001, where a review found his abuse likely continued until his death in Cape Town in 2018. The Makin Review, published in November 2024, found an "active cover-up" in England, called Smyth "a problem solved and exported to Africa", and found no sign that anyone had tried to warn Zimbabwean authorities. Archbishop Justin Welby resigned days later.

Children had been sent from Britain to the same country decades earlier. Between 1946 and 1956, 276 British child migrants were sent to the Rhodesia Fairbridge Memorial College in what is now Zimbabwe. A UK inquiry found that children who told the headmaster a padre had sexually abused them were beaten and warned against "spreading malicious lies". Its wider 2018 report called child migration "a deeply flawed government policy".

Today the US 2025 trafficking report describes girls and women exploited around gold and diamond mines, sometimes for money or food, and children used as panners and ore couriers. It notes that some families trade daughters for food or money, and that under ngozi, a girl may be given to another family to atone for a killing. It reports low-level official complicity.

Sending an abuser abroad can end the problem for the institution that sends him while starting it for children somewhere else. Ask whether anyone at the receiving end was told.

AFG.story:
In 2011 a US Army sergeant, Charles Martland, and his captain, Dan Quinn, beat an Afghan Local Police commander who had admitted chaining and raping a 12-year-old boy. Quinn was relieved of command and Martland was at first separated from the army. The commander was an ally. The practice he was part of is called bacha bazi: boys abused by Afghan commanders.

In September 2015 the New York Times reported that US soldiers had been told to ignore such abuse by Afghan allies, in some cases even on US bases. Nearly 100 members of Congress asked the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction (SIGAR) to investigate. Its report, made public in January 2018, found the Pentagon had been tracking 75 gross human rights violations by Afghan security forces from 2010 to 2016, at least seven of them child sexual assault, and said the full extent "may never be known". US law, the Leahy Law, requires cutting aid to units that commit such abuses. The Pentagon used an exception in that law to keep funding implicated units, including 12 units linked to 14 violations in December 2015.

After the Taliban took power, the UN verified sexual violence against 12 children in 2023, 10 of the cases attributed to the Taliban, and 3 children abducted by the Taliban for sexual purposes. In 2024 boys aged 10 to 17 at Taliban-run madrasahs, religious schools, told Radio Azadi that teachers pressured them into sexual acts. One 16-year-old reported a teacher to the school's head, who only told the teacher to stop; the teacher continued. A UN report counted 6,836 such madrasahs for boys.

No representative survey anywhere in South Asia measures online child sexual exploitation, so that side of the problem has no figures at all.

When abusers are useful to a government, whether as allies or as the government itself, reporting has nowhere to go. Ask who decided the abuse was someone else's business, and what that decision cost.

MDA.story:
In the late 1990s, girls and women from Moldova were sold to bar owners in post-war Bosnia and held in debt bondage. A 2002 Human Rights Watch report found local police acting as brothel owners, guards and clients. Eighteen UN police monitors who bought women, visited brothels or faced trafficking charges were sent home, and none was confirmed prosecuted. A US Army report documented contractors from the firm DynCorp buying women; one confessed to buying a woman, along with an Uzi, for 1,600 Deutschmarks. DynCorp fired Kathryn Bolkovac, the monitor who reported it, and a British tribunal later found the dismissal unfair. In Kosovo, Amnesty International found in 2004 that NATO troops and UN staff generated 80% of traffickers' income, and that women and girls were brought in mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia. Amnesty found no criminal cases against any soldiers in their home countries.

Moldova was a source, not a destination. In 2007 the US State Department reported women and children trafficked from Moldova to Russia, Turkey, Israel and the UAE. UNICEF found children leaving Moldova's residential institutions were several times more vulnerable to trafficking than other children. The 2025 US report says the same group is still targeted, now often through social media, video chat and fake job ads, with abuse images used to groom children. Moldovan courts convicted 33 traffickers in 2024; a former police officer was among those convicted, of labour trafficking.

Moldova also hosts abuse material online. The Internet Watch Foundation actioned 9,941 web addresses hosted there in 2025, 3% of its total.

The buyers in these cases, from peacekeepers to contractors, were mostly sent home rather than tried. Notice which children are targeted first: those leaving state care with no family to look for them.

VAT.story:
In August 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Polish Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, amid allegations that he had abused minors. Dominican prosecutors opened their criminal investigation only afterwards, on 4 September, by which time he was out of their reach in Vatican City. A church tribunal found him guilty, and he was laicised, removed from the priesthood, in June 2014. In June 2015 a Vatican prosecutor indicted him for abusing children in the Dominican Republic and possessing abuse images. He was found dead in his Vatican rooms that August, before trial. A Polish priest who had worked alongside him, Fr Wojciech Gil, returned to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic; a Polish court sentenced him to seven years.

The pattern repeated. In 2017 the Holy See recalled Mgr Carlo Capella, a diplomat at its Washington embassy, after he was accused of handling abuse images. He was tried not in the US or Canada but by a Vatican tribunal, which convicted him in 2018 and gave him five years and a €5,000 fine. Its ambassador to France, Archbishop Luigi Ventura, was tried in Paris in his absence and given an eight-month suspended sentence in 2020.

Rome also received clergy facing complaints elsewhere. Fr Bernard Prince was appointed to Rome in 1991, and a 1993 church letter discussed keeping him hidden in the Vatican rather than facing justice in Canada. Argentine Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta resigned amid complaints in 2017 and was given a Vatican post that December; Argentina convicted him in 2022 of abusing two adult seminarians.

When Ireland's Murphy Commission sought files in 2009, the Holy See supplied none. The map also lists its dealings with inquiries in England and Wales (2020) and Poland (2022) under the same pattern.

Because the Holy See is a state, it can call its diplomats home and try them in its own courts. Ask whether victims' countries ever got the chance to try the accused themselves.

IDN.story:
In July 2025 police in West Java said a syndicate had sold at least 25 babies since 2023, mostly to buyers in Singapore. Some babies were "reserved while still in the womb". They sold for 11–16 million rupiah each, after the group prepared false family cards and passports in Pontianak. Thirteen people were arrested, six babies about to be sent were rescued, and police asked Interpol to help trace the adopters.

This trade has a longer history. In 2021 a Dutch government inquiry found "serious violations" in adoptions from countries including Indonesia between 1967 and 1998, and concluded that Dutch officials had known of wrongdoing for years without intervening. The Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoptions that February.

Offenders also come to Indonesia. The US 2025 trafficking report says child sexual exploitation by foreigners is common in the Riau Islands across the water from Singapore, and that women and girls are coerced into commercial sex in Batam. In 2017 Batam police arrested a Singaporean man accused of molesting three boys. In Puncak, near Bogor, the report says tourists from the Middle East pay more than $700 for week-long "contract marriages" with girls as young as nine, a practice it says the government tacitly accepted. It adds that corruption and complicity significantly held back efforts to stop trafficking.

A "contract marriage" or a forged family card gives an exploitative deal the look of a legal one. Ask who issues the paperwork and who benefits from not looking closely at it.

PRT.story:
In 1975 a teacher at Casa Pia, Portugal's state institution caring for about 4,500 children in Lisbon, began reporting abuse of boys to its leaders and to police. In 1981 police accused a caretaker. Neither report led to legal action. One of the men later convicted, the diplomat Jorge Ritto, had been removed as consul in Stuttgart around 1969–71 after a complaint about an under-age boy, but stayed in the diplomatic service.

The case came to light in 2002, 27 years after the teacher's first report. A trial began in 2004 and ended on 3 September 2010 with six of seven defendants convicted. Carlos Silvino, a former Casa Pia driver, confessed to 639 charges of abusing boys or procuring them for others and received 18 years. TV presenter Carlos Cruz and doctor João Ferreira Diniz got seven years each, Ritto six years and eight months, lawyer Hugo Marçal six years and two months, and former Casa Pia governor Manuel Abrantes five years and nine months. The convicted men other than Silvino denied the charges. A woman accused of letting her house be used was acquitted. Former minister Paulo Pedroso was detained during the investigation but not tried.

The Catholic Church in Portugal looked at itself much later. A commission set up by the bishops and led by child psychiatrist Pedro Strecht reported in February 2023, after more than 500 survivors gave testimony, that at least 4,815 children had been abused in the church since 1950. Most offences were past the legal deadline for prosecution; 25 cases went to prosecutors.

At Casa Pia the children were in the state's own care, and the warnings came from inside the institution. When a complaint is made and nothing happens, ask who received it and what their connection was to the accused.

GAB.story:
In 2014 and 2015, in the town of Dékoa in the Central African Republic, UN peacekeepers from Gabon and Burundi were deployed to protect civilians. The UN's 2017 report says two allegations against these troops led to interviews of some 136 alleged victims, 48% of all victims the UN recorded in 2016. Investigations were left to the troops' home countries, and those were still pending. Press accounts reported that at least 98 girls described abuse and that 41 troops were identified and sent home without charges.

The allegations did not stop. On 15 September 2021 the UN announced it would send home all Gabonese military units in the mission, about 450 personnel, after new allegations of sexual exploitation and abuse. Gabon opened an investigation. The UN's 2022 report linked most of the mission's multiple-victim allegations of 2021 to one troop-contributing country repatriated that September.

Inside Gabon, little is measured. No representative survey in West and Central Africa tracks online child sexual exploitation, so there are no figures on how often it happens there.

Sending troops home ends the UN's problem but leaves prosecution to the same government that sent them. Ask what happened to the soldiers after they landed.

MOZ.story:
After Mozambique's 1992 peace treaty, the UN sent a peacekeeping mission, ONUMOZ, to help the country through the end of its civil war. A UN study led by Graça Machel, published in August 1996, found that ONUMOZ soldiers had recruited girls aged 12 to 18 into prostitution. The study looked at 12 countries and found that in six of them the arrival of peacekeeping troops was linked to a rapid rise in child prostitution.

Decades later the war in the north brought a different danger. In Cabo Delgado province, armed groups linked to the Islamic State have been taking children. The UN verified 468 abductions of children there in 2024, 371 boys and 97 girls, most of them to be used as fighters or helpers, and sexual violence against 5 girls. In 2023 it verified sexual violence against 12 girls, and the perpetrators were not only the armed groups: 5 cases were attributed to Mozambique's own armed forces and 3 to a police rapid intervention unit.

In both periods, some of the abuse came from the forces sent to protect civilians. When soldiers or police arrive in a crisis zone, ask who is watching how they treat children and who can hold them to account.

SLE.story:
In 1998, during Sierra Leone's civil war, about 29 children staying at a centre in Makeni run by a group called Help A Needy Child International (HANCI) were taken to Freetown for what parents were told were medical checks. The children never came back. Their parents later learned they had been adopted by families in the United States.

Adoptions to the US went on. Between 1994 and 2014 the US issued 385 immigrant visas to children adopted from Sierra Leone, with a peak of 56 in 2003. Sierra Leone suspended adoptions on 21 May 2009. In April 2012 a presidential commission shut HANCI down and concluded that the Makeni families "cannot be said to have genuinely consented".

Other kinds of abuse are harder to see. No representative survey anywhere in West and Central Africa measures online child sexual exploitation, so there are no figures for Sierra Leone.

Parents can lose a child through a form they did not understand or were never shown. Ask what the families were told, and who checked that they agreed.

WSM.story:
Between 2002 and 2005, a Utah adoption agency called Focus on Children, run by Scott and Karen Banks, approached families in Samoa. Parents were told their children would go to the United States for a time to attend school. About 80 children went, and they were adopted permanently. In February 2007 a federal indictment charged the Banks couple and three others with alien smuggling, visa fraud and money laundering. In January 2009 all pleaded guilty to minor charges of helping a foreigner enter the US improperly, and the agency to a felony conspiracy. The judge sentenced them to five years' probation and banned them from adoption work. No one went to prison.

Samoa also appears as a place where abusers were sent. A Salesian priest convicted of abuse in Melbourne, Australia, was allegedly moved to Samoa to avoid further police investigation.

Samoan families had no way to check what happened to their children once they reached the US. Ask what families were promised in writing, and compare it with the papers they were asked to sign.

GRL.story:
In May 1951 Danish authorities, working with Save the Children Denmark, had teachers and priests in Greenland pick out children aged six to ten. Twenty-two Inuit children were sent to foster families in Denmark to be re-educated as "little Danes". Many of their families were reluctant. About a year and a half later, 16 of the children returned to Greenland, but they were placed in a children's home built by the Danish Red Cross, and many never lived with their families again. The other six were adopted in Denmark.

A report in 2020 found that half of the children later had mental health problems. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen apologised in December 2020. In March 2022, after the survivors took legal action, the six still living were each awarded 250,000 kroner.

This was a government plan carried out openly, with charities' help, in the name of the children's future. When a state removes children to change who they become, ask who chose them, what the families were allowed to say, and how long it took for anyone to apologise.

URY.story:
In August 1976 a pregnant 19-year-old Argentine woman was detained in Buenos Aires. Under Operation Condor, a pact between South American military governments, she was moved secretly to Montevideo. She gave birth in a military hospital. In December 1976 her baby was taken from her and left with a police officer's family, who raised the girl under another name for 23 years. The mother disappeared.

In 1986 Uruguay passed the Expiry Law, an amnesty for crimes committed under military rule. It was used to close the investigation into this case in 2003. On 24 February 2011 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights found Uruguay responsible for the mother's disappearance and for erasing the child's identity, and ruled the amnesty law had no legal effect in this case.

In this case the child was taken by state agents and given to a police officer's family. Notice how amnesty laws can close cases, and ask who decides when a past crime may be investigated again.

SLV.story:
In 1982, during El Salvador's civil war, the army carried out an operation known as the "Guinda de Mayo". Two young sisters from the Serrano Cruz family disappeared during it. In 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled on their case.

They were two of many. Pro-Búsqueda, a group founded in 1994 to search for missing children, has documented close to a thousand children who disappeared during the war, mostly taken by the armed forces. Many were adopted, through flawed procedures, by families in the United States, France, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands. El Salvador set up a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children in 2010. The armed forces have still not opened their archives on the missing children despite years of requests.

When children vanish in a war and reappear abroad as adoptees, the records of who took them are the key to finding them. Ask who holds those records and why they remain closed.

ALB.story:
Each summer, as tourists arrive on Albania's coast, the US 2025 trafficking report says traffickers exploit Albanian women and children in sex trafficking and forced labour. Roma and Balkan-Egyptian children are forced to beg. Albanians who migrate to Western Europe, especially the UK, are vulnerable to being forced into crime; in 2024 Albanians were the second most common nationality referred in the UK as possible trafficking victims, 2,492 people, though 95 per cent of them were referred as adults.

For years these cases did not reach a verdict at home. In the period the report covers, Albanian courts convicted two sex traffickers and two labour traffickers, the first trafficking convictions since 2021.

Four convictions in a year, after several years with none, is the whole court record in this packet. Ask how many cases were reported compared with how many reached a judge.

TZA.story:
On Zanzibar, the US 2025 trafficking report says, girls and women from the Tanzanian mainland are brought to the islands with false promises and then exploited. Children there are sexually exploited, including by visiting foreigners, and held in forced labour and domestic work. The report names other places where child sex trafficking also happens: Arusha, Dar es Salaam, Dodoma, Mbeya and Mwanza. The people involved include brokers and foster families, not only strangers.

The report says the government did not do enough about corruption and officials' involvement. It gives no count of victims, and no case in this packet has reached a court.

When the main record of a problem is a foreign government's yearly report, the local picture is thin. Ask who in the country is counting these children, and what happens when an official is accused.

SEN.story:
In Kédougou, a gold-mining region in Senegal's south-east, the US 2025 trafficking report says organised networks bring Nigerian women and girls, some as young as 12, for sex trafficking. The same networks move them to mining areas in Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire.

Beyond this, almost nothing is measured. Childlight, a research group that tracks child sexual exploitation, found in 2026 that West and Central Africa have no representative survey data on abuse carried out through phones and the internet. So there is no figure for how many children in Senegal are affected online.

An empty space in the data means no one has counted, not that nothing happened. Ask whether any survey of children's safety has been done in Senegal, and who would pay for one.

MYS.story:
In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a UK group that finds and removes child sexual abuse material online, took action on 17,046 web addresses hosted on servers in Malaysia. That was 5% of everything it actioned that year, the same share as in 2024. Hosting means the files sit on computers in the country, even if the people who made, sell or view them are elsewhere.

This packet has no Malaysian court cases or inquiries to explain who runs these servers or who pays for them. The figure shows where the material is stored, not where the children are.

When a country keeps appearing on hosting lists year after year, ask which companies own the servers, how quickly they remove material when told, and whether any law makes them act.

CIV.story:
For Côte d'Ivoire, this map has no case, inquiry or court record to tell. What it has is a gap. Childlight, a research group that tracks child sexual exploitation, found in 2026 that West and Central Africa have no representative survey data on child sexual abuse carried out through phones and the internet. Without such surveys, no one can say how many children in the country are groomed, blackmailed or filmed online.

A survey of this kind asks a random sample of young people what has happened to them, which is how other regions have produced their estimates. Where it has never been done, there is no estimate to compare against reported cases.

An empty space on this map means no one has counted, not that nothing happened. Ask whether any national survey of children's safety has ever been carried out, and who would pay for one.

PRK.story:
In 2025 the US National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, which receives reports of online child sexual abuse from internet companies worldwide, logged 12 reports for North Korea.

The center itself reads this as a near-total absence of data: the low number reflects how few people in North Korea can get online, not how often children there are abused. No other source on this map fills the gap.

A near-zero count here describes a country cut off from the internet, not a safe one. When reading any country's figures, ask first whether the reporting channels could reach it at all.
